policy: Preserve reviewed Matthew and all checkpointed chapter alignments during automated repair and deployment. Review both alignment directions. Corrected records a bilingual correction pass; verified requires explicit final bilingual verification and regression evidence. Record deployment separately with evidence. Certification requires verification and successful deployment of the same chapter content. Resume at the recorded chapter.

reviewed_advisory_lexical_flags: 2:28 Jew, (9) — The Greek noun is represented by the first Jew. The English repeats it as a predicative complement.
2:28 circumcision, (16) — The Greek noun is represented by the first circumcision. The English supplies its repetition as a predicate.
3:8 say— (3) — The initial say completes the elliptical English question. The Greek λέγειν renders the second say in we say.
3:29 God (4) — The single θεὸς is the first God. DGT repeats God in its predicative phrase.
6:19 terms (5) — The word terms is supplied as the nominal head in the adverbial English expression in human terms.
7:1 person (28) — The Greek ἀνθρώπου renders the earlier person. The repeated noun makes the subject of lives explicit in English.
10:12 Lord (14) — The single κύριος is represented by the first Lord. DGT supplies the second Lord as a predicate.
11:18 supports (21) — βαστάζεις is the preceding second-person support. DGT supplies supports after the root in the elliptical contrast.
11:31 shown (9) — Shown is supplied in the first clause as part of the rendering of your mercy. The candidate ἐλεηθῶσιν is already rendered by may receive mercy in the second clause.
12:9 Let (0) — The Greek is a verbless clause. English supplies a hortative verb, and ἀγάπη renders love.
13:7 due, (11) — ὀφειλάς renders the earlier what is owed. English supplies is due in the first obligation phrase.
14:4 servant’s (10) — The possessive servant’s is a second reference to the servant introduced in the previous sentence. The later ἰδίῳ renders own.
14:5 alike. (12) — ἡμέραν renders day. English supplies alike to express the implication of judging every day.
16:5 greet (1) — English repeats the greeting verb from the preceding sentence. The local ἀσπάσασθε belongs to the greeting of Epaenetus.
